items.q: How quickly can I be registered with AHPRA?
items.a: Allow at least six weeks once AHPRA has a complete application, and longer for some pathways. If your specialty requires a college assessment first, that adds time before AHPRA can start. We build a realistic timeline with you at the outset and handle any follow-up questions from AHPRA so your file keeps moving.

items.q: Will I have to pass AMC exams?
items.a: Only on some pathways. AMC exams are usually part of the Standard pathway, but doctors on the Competent Authority, Expedited Specialist or Specialist pathways normally skip them. Bear in mind you may still need to complete a period of supervised practice once you start work.

items.q: Which type of medical registration will I hold?
items.a: It depends on your pathway. Provisional registration covers a period of supervised practice and is the usual starting point on the Competent Authority pathway. Limited registration is tied to a particular role, purpose or program and often carries conditions. General registration lets you work across your scope of practice, and specialist registration recognises you as a specialist in an approved field. Many IMGs start on provisional or limited registration and progress from there.

items.q: Is the Expedited Specialist Pathway the same as RACGP Fellowship?
items.a: No. The Expedited Specialist Pathway (ESP) leads to specialist registration with AHPRA and specialist recognition with Medicare, but it is not Fellowship of the RACGP and is not a pathway to Fellowship. You can apply to the RACGP for Fellowship separately later on.

Under section 19AB of the Health Insurance Act 1973, most IMGs must work in a Distribution Priority Area (DPA), or a District of Workforce Shortage for specialists, to access Medicare benefits for up to ten years from their first Australian medical registration. Some exemptions apply, such as the spousal exemption. We'll advise on the options available to you.

items.q: Can my partner and children come with me?
items.a: Usually, yes. The main employer-sponsored visas for doctors, the Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) and the Employer Nomination Scheme visa (subclass 186), let you include a spouse or partner and dependent children who meet the criteria. What they can do in Australia, such as work or study, depends on the visa. Our migration agents check each family member's eligibility and lodge their applications with yours.

items.q: Which documents need to be certified or translated?
items.a: You'll need certified copies of the documents for each application. If you're outside Australia, they must be certified by a Notary Public. Any document not in English needs a full certified English translation. Your regulatory consultant will give you a checklist and tell you when to order items such as Certificates of Good Standing and criminal history checks.

items.q: We've found a doctor ourselves. Can you still manage the paperwork?
items.a: Absolutely. You don't need to recruit through Wavelength to use our regulatory and migration services. Many health services engage us purely to handle registration, Medicare and visas for doctors they've hired directly.

items.q: Do you handle visa sponsorship for employers?
items.a: Yes. Our MARA-registered migration agents confirm whether your organisation can sponsor, choose the right visa and manage sponsorship, nomination and visa applications, timed to line up with the doctor's registration.

items.q: What does sponsoring a doctor on a Skills in Demand (482) visa involve?
items.a: Three applications: sponsorship (your practice is approved as a Standard Business Sponsor, if it isn't already), nomination (the position is approved, with a Skilling Australians Fund levy for each nominated year) and the visa itself. If you're not yet an approved sponsor, you'll need to show your business is actively operating, including financials. We prepare and lodge each step for you.

items.q: How long does the whole registration and visa process take?
items.a: It depends on the pathway. As a guide, registration and visa together take around five months on the Expedited Specialist Pathway and six to twelve months on the RACGP Practice Experience Program, depending on regulator and Department of Home Affairs workloads. We keep you updated at every stage.

items.q: What supervision will an overseas-trained doctor need?
items.a: It varies with the doctor's pathway, experience and role, and with any conditions set by the Medical Board of Australia or the specialist college. We'll tell you what applies before you make an offer, so you can confirm a suitable supervisor early. Email rms@wave.com.au to talk it through.

items.q: How do the four supervision levels work?
items.a: Supervision runs from Level 1 to Level 4, with the doctor taking on more responsibility at each step. At Level 1 the supervisor is directly responsible for every patient and must be on site. At Level 2 responsibility is shared, and the supervisor is physically present most of the time. At Level 3 the doctor takes primary responsibility and can work alone, with the supervisor contactable by phone or video. At Level 4 the doctor is fully responsible, with the supervisor reviewing their practice periodically.
